Let me look at specific features. The bicycle tire (the big horizontal one) - in the first image, the tire's vertical center is around the middle. In the second image, the tire appears to be at a similar or slightly lower position? Hmm.

That would mean the camera moved up (translated up), revealing more of the bottom? Wait, if the camera translates up, the view shifts up, meaning objects move down in the frame, and we see more of the top? Hmm, need to think.

Camera translation: If the camera moves up (physically up), then the scene appears to move down in the image. So we'd see more of the top of the scene at the top edge? No wait. Let's think carefully.

Imagine a fixed scene. The camera is a window looking at the scene. If the camera moves up, the window moves up, so the part of the scene that was at the top of the window is now above the window (out of view), and the part that was below comes into view at the bottom. So in the image, the scene content appears to shift downward. Objects move down in the frame.

Conversely, if the camera moves down, the scene content appears to shift upward in the frame.

Now compare the two images. Let's track a feature, say the big horizontal tire. In image 1, the tire's top edge is around y=420 and bottom edge around y=550. In image 2, the tire's top edge is around y=420 and bottom edge around y=560. Hmm similar.

Simpler: track a single feature's pixel position between the two images. If the feature's pixel y decreased (moved toward top of image) in image 2, then the camera moved... If camera moves down by dh, the center of the image (optical axis) moves down in world, meaning it now points at a lower part of the world? So the center of the image now corresponds to a lower world point. In the image, a fixed world point P was at some image position; after camera moves down, the world point that maps to image center is lower. So P, which was higher than the new center, would appear higher in the image? Let's do math.

Let world vertical coordinate be Y (down positive). Camera optical axis points in some direction; assume for simplicity camera looks horizontally at a vertical wall, but here it's a floor so let's just consider vertical component. Ugh.

Let's just use the simple rule: camera moves in direction D, scene appears to move in image in direction -D (opposite), for translation perpendicular to optical axis. This is the standard "camera moves right => scene moves left" rule. So camera moves down => scene moves up in image. Yes that's the rule: the apparent motion of the scene is opposite to the camera's motion. So if features in image 2 are higher (smaller y) than in image 1, the scene moved up, so camera moved down.
